items.title: Linus Torvalds is Angry Again, This Time With ext4 Dev
items.summary: "You are full of crap". Linux creator Linus Torvalds gets angry at ext4 maintainer.
items.body:
Theodore Ts'o, who maintains ext4, sent Linus Torvalds a pull request of 94 commits for Linux 7.4-rc5, and the merge commit that followed adds 41,204 lines across 68 files.

Ts'o said KUnit tests make up most of the added code and exist to help validate patches that AI generates, and that most of the bug fixes in the pull were AI generated as well.

What was in the pull that got Torvalds all worked up?

Before we dive into that, know that the ext4 filesystem grew out of ext3 and was built to be reliable and to scale to large storage, including filesystems larger than 16TB.

Whereas KUnit is the kernel's unit testing framework, where tests are written in C and run against kernel code at boot or as a module.

The tests in Ts'o's pull account for 22 of the 68 changed files in the merge commit. The rest is bug fixes and three minor performance changes.

One performance change spreads the inodes of files in sibling directories over a flex group's block groups and speeds up parallel file creation. Another moves the orphan list fields off a shared cache line, and a third skips holes when replaying fast commits for sparse files.

The bug fixes include data loss cases, such as fsync'ed data lost after a journal flush and data lost during ext3 inode migration.

Others cover stale data after a failed zeroout, use-after-free bugs, out-of-bounds accesses on corrupted filesystems and a readdir problem with large directories on 32-bit kernels.

Torvalds objected to 41,197 lines of code being added so late in release cycle

Kernel development works in cycles, with new code going in during a merge window of about two weeks. The weekly release candidates that follow, called "rc" builds, are meant for fixes, and a cycle usually reaches somewhere between rc6 and rc9.

Torvalds objected that a pull of this size belongs in the merge window and that calling something a fix does not make it fit for an rc.

He said more than 41,000 added lines can cause new problems even when most of them are tests or fixes for other bugs. Fixes for old, subtle bugs can bring bugs of their own too, whether a person or an AI wrote them.

He took the pull after thinking about dropping it, and he closed his reply with a warning to Ts'o:

Get your shit together and stop this kind of
idiocy.

And tell your AI companion to get its act together, and do any new development and test-cases ON A SEPARATE DAMN BRANCH, so that it can be merged during the MERGE WINDOW.

What's so hard to understand about this?

How it ended

Ts'o replied that the tests were already on their own branch and had been placed at the end of the pull so they could be dropped easily. He offered to send a new pull request without them and hold the tests back until the next merge window opened.

Torvalds answered that he still partly objected, but he kept the merge. The conflicts from the test changes were not enough to make him undo it.

What Linus has said before

Torvalds complained in May about a bloated rc with pointless pull requests, much of it AI assisted, and promised to be tougher. But he has also said Linux is not one of those anti-AI projects.

By his count, the 7.4 merge window brought almost 20,000 commits against the roughly 15,000 that is typical. He would rather get AI fixes there than late in an rc, and he hopes they become mundane.

translation.title: Linus Torvalds 又发火了，这次是针对 ext4 开发者
translation.summary: “你满嘴胡扯”。Linux 创始人 Linus Torvalds 对 ext4 维护者发火。
translation.label: 机器翻译
translation.summary_source: "You are full of crap". Linux creator Linus Torvalds gets angry at ext4 maintainer.
translation.body:
维护 ext4 的 Theodore Ts'o 向 Linus Torvalds 提交了一个包含 94 个提交的拉取请求，用于 Linux 7.4-rc5，随后的合并提交在 68 个文件中新增了 41,204 行代码。

Ts'o 表示，新增代码大部分是 KUnit 测试，这些测试用于帮助验证 AI 生成的补丁，而且该拉取请求中的大部分缺陷修复也是 AI 生成的。

这个拉取请求里究竟是什么让 Torvalds 如此恼火？

在深入讨论之前，需要知道 ext4 文件系统是从 ext3 发展而来的，其设计目标是可靠性和可扩展到大容量存储，包括大于 16TB 的文件系统。

而 KUnit 是内核的单元测试框架，测试用 C 语言编写，在启动时或作为模块针对内核代码运行。

Ts'o 的拉取请求中的测试占合并提交中 68 个变更文件中的 22 个。其余是缺陷修复和三项小幅性能改进。

一项性能改进将同级目录中文件的 inode 分散到一个 flex group 的块组上，从而加快并行文件创建。另一项将孤儿列表字段移出共享缓存行，第三项在对稀疏文件重放快速提交时跳过空洞。

缺陷修复包括数据丢失情况，例如日志刷新后已 fsync 的数据丢失，以及 ext3 inode 迁移期间的数据丢失。

其他修复涵盖清零失败后的陈旧数据、释放后使用缺陷、损坏文件系统上的越界访问，以及 32 位内核上大目录的 readdir 问题。

Torvalds 反对在发布周期如此晚的阶段新增 41,197 行代码

内核开发按周期进行，新代码在约两周的合并窗口期间进入。随后的每周候选版本称为“rc”版本，用于修复，一个周期通常达到 rc6 到 rc9 之间。

Torvalds 反对说，这种规模的拉取请求应属于合并窗口，而且把某样东西称为修复并不能使其适合 rc。

他说，超过 41,000 行新增代码可能引发新问题，即使其中大部分是测试或其他缺陷的修复。对旧的、隐蔽缺陷的修复也可能带来自身的缺陷，无论作者是人还是 AI。

他在考虑放弃后还是接受了该拉取请求，并在回复结尾警告 Ts'o：

把你的烂摊子收拾好，别再干这种
蠢事。

还要告诉你的 AI 伙伴端正态度，任何新开发和测试用例都要放在一个单独的该死分支上，以便能在合并窗口期间合并。

这有什么难理解的？

结局如何

Ts'o 回复说，测试已经放在单独分支上，并被放在拉取请求末尾以便轻松丢弃。他提出可以发送一个不含这些测试的新拉取请求，并将测试推迟到下一个合并窗口开启。

Torvalds 回答说，他仍部分反对，但他保留了这次合并。测试变更引发的冲突不足以让他撤销合并。

Linus 此前说过什么

Torvalds 在 5 月曾抱怨一个臃肿的 rc 包含无意义的拉取请求，其中很多是 AI 辅助的，并承诺会更严格。但他也表示 Linux 不属于那些反 AI 的项目。

据他统计，7.4 合并窗口带来了近 20,000 个提交，而通常约为 15,000 个。他更愿意在那里收到 AI 修复，而不是在 rc 后期，并希望它们变得司空见惯。

items.title: Meet Warty, the AI Launcher Canonical Is Building for Ubuntu
items.summary: Ubuntu's AI launcher should be available in January. Every AI feature introduced is being strictly opt-in and local-first.
items.body:
Back in April, Canonical shared its plans for AI in Ubuntu, favoring models that run on the user's own hardware and open-weight options over cloud services.

The plan also split AI features as behind-the-scenes improvements to existing parts of the OS and visible, as well as agentic ones that users opt into.

Myna came next, a speech-to-text tool that runs on local models. It debuted as an optional preview in Ubuntu 26.10, and the company says it will ship by default with Ubuntu 28.04 LTS.

More recently, Canonical introduced Surge at Ubuntu Summit 26.10. The AI system writes and checks security fixes for Ubuntu packages, and those fixes are offered through an opt-in archive for Ubuntu Pro users instead of reaching stable releases automatically.

Now the newest step in this direction is an AI-powered launcher.

It first showed up as a simulated snap on the Snap Store in October, and Didier Roche, the developer working on it, has now explained where the project is headed.

An AI-powered launcher?

Current status of Warty Launcher. (Source: Didier Roche)

The aim of this new launcher (warty-launcher) is to provide a single spot on the desktop for finding files, opening apps, and getting help from an AI model on request.

Both typing and talking are input types that are to be supported. ⌨️🗣️

Unlike the October prototype snap, the launcher now actually runs and has some functionality built into it, with Canonical publishing its technical design and first public release in January 2027.

Alongside that, testing also opens, and the developers are looking forward to collecting feedback on their design choices.

Didier also mentions that turning on AI is the user's choice, with the traditional app launcher staying the default experience for anyone who prefers it.

Additionally, large AI models will not come bundled with the default install for Warty Launcher.

Anyone who opts in is meant to get inference on their own machine ahead of remote servers, with personal files, session context, etc. not leaving the machine.

The parts that power it are built to stay isolated under Ubuntu's confinement tools to protect the host system.

However, the announcement does not name the models or the hardware requirements, and some foundational work still has to be finished first.

A brief demo

After launching the prototype Snap package for Warty Launcher, a small button appears at the top right of the screen inside the top panel with shortcuts for Clipboard, Emoji, Files, and Tasks.

If you remember from earlier, Didier's post shows a newer build that places the launcher near the top center instead; I prefer the newer approach.

The Clipboard mode lists recent copies with the app and time each one came from. The sample entries include a restaurant booking, a hotel address, and a train ticket screenshot, and a follow-up button next to the search field hands any of them to the AI.

The latest build of Warty Launcher. (Source: Diedier Roche)

Once I sent a test prompt through the follow-up, it showed a "Working on this device" message and then returned lorem ipsum filler as the answer. This was a given, as the Snap store listing for the prototype says actions are simulated.

Emoji shows a grid of recent picks. Files waits for three characters before it offers to open a match or show it in the file manager, and Tasks keeps a list of what the launcher has done, such as opening files.

Test it yourself

If you want to try it yourself, the snap is only available on the edge channel and installs via a single command:

sudo snap install warty-prototype --edge

Once it is installed, running warty-prototype in a terminal starts it and opens the launcher.

A few GTK and graphics warnings showed up in my terminal, but the launcher still appeared. To close it, pick "Quit the prototype" from the right-click menu in the top panel.

This is a standalone prototype with simulated actions and demo data. If you are hoping to use it, give it a few more weeks before it matures into a daily-use kind of feature.

Warty Launcher (prototype)

items.title: Local AI Weekly #11: Local AI Grows Up
items.summary: Local AI adoption keeps on growing.
items.body:
For a long time, running AI locally felt like a weekend project. But things are getting serious. Local AI projects are maturing with each release.

llama.cpp, the engine under almost everything local, finally hit version 1.0. LocalAI shipped a release that wants to do actual office work. Even the new tools look like proper apps rather than early demos.

Local AI is growing up. Let's see what that looks like.

🎓 The grown-up releases

llama.cpp 1.0 arrived a few days ago. After years of build numbers in the thousands, it finally has a proper version. It's a cleanup release too, with 36 deprecated API functions removed.

There are new features as well. You can now store the KV cache in "FP8" with -ctk f8_e4m3 -ctv f8_e4m3, which saves memory on long chats. MoE models get a host memory cache for experts, so big mixture of experts models behave better when they don't fully fit in VRAM.

LocalAI 5.0 also came out a few days ago and its pitch is that you can "give real work to a model you run yourself." Well, every AI tool wants to do real work these than just being your chat partner.

LocalAI 5.0: your AI does the work, you keep the files

Run open models for chat, images, speech and video on your own machines. The API speaks the OpenAI and Anthropic formats. 5.0 adds Projects, a desktop app for macOS and Linux, and documents, files and team sharing.

LocalAIEttore Di Giacinto

🖥 On my desk

Last week was all about dictation, and I'm still on it. Right now I'm testing Quoth, an offline voice dictation app for Linux. You press a shortcut, speak, and the text gets pasted into whatever app you're using. It's basically Wispr Flow without your voice leaving your computer. Stay tuned for a full hands-on review video.

🔍 Discover AI tools

whichllm answers the question every local AI beginner asks: what can my machine run? It reads your GPU, RAM and memory bandwidth, estimates which open models fit and how fast they'll be, then ranks them by benchmark scores.

Next on my test list is Snippai, an AGPL-licensed snipping tool. You grab a part of your screen and it turns formulas into LaTeX, tables into Markdown, or explains the code in a screenshot. Basically, a local AI-based OCR tool. I will share how it performs next week.

GitHub - xyTom/snippai at itsfoss.com

Snip Anything Solve Everything​. Contribute to xyTom/snippai development by creating an account on GitHub.

GitHub

🗂 AI jargon: FP8

You came across FP8 in this newsletter already, so I thought of explaining the term.

FP8 is an 8-bit floating point number format. Most models store numbers in 16 bits (FP16 or BF16), so FP8 uses half the memory for the same data.

Of course, there is a trade-off for this and that trade-off is precision, since fewer bits means rougher numbers. For things like the KV cache, the "short-term memory" of a chat, the quality loss is usually small and the memory savings are big. That's why llama.cpp 1.0 adding FP8 KV caches matters on consumer GPUs.

⚡ Quick Tip

Not sure which model to pull next? If you have uv installed, you can run whichllm without installing anything:

uvx whichllm@latest

It checks your hardware and gives you a ranked list of models that will actually fit. If your integrated GPU or unified memory gets detected wrong, use --vram to set the limits yourself.

See you next week 🙂

LocalAI 5.0 also came out a few days ago and its pitch is that you can "give real work to a model you run yourself." Well, every AI tool wants to do real work these than just being your chat partner.
LocalAI 5.0: your AI does the work, you keep the files

Run open models for chat, images, speech and video on your own machines. The API speaks the OpenAI and Anthropic formats. 5.0 adds Projects, a desktop app for macOS and Linux, and documents, files and team sharing.
LocalAIEttore Di Giacinto
🖥 On my desk

Last week was all about dictation, and I'm still on it. Right now I'm testing Quoth, an offline voice dictation app for Linux. You press a shortcut, speak, and the text gets pasted into whatever app you're using. It's basically Wispr Flow without your voice leaving your computer. Stay tuned for a full hands-on review video.
🔍 Discover AI tools

whichllm answers the question every local AI beginner asks: what can my machine run? It reads your GPU, RAM and memory bandwidth, estimates which open models fit and how fast they'll be, then ranks them by benchmark scores.

Next on my test list is Snippai, an AGPL-licensed snipping tool. You grab a part of your screen and it turns formulas into LaTeX, tables into Markdown, or explains the code in a screenshot. Basically, a local AI-based OCR tool. I will share how it performs next week.
GitHub - xyTom/snippai at itsfoss.com
Snip Anything Solve Everything​. Contribute to xyTom/snippai development by creating an account on GitHub.
GitHub
🗂 AI jargon: FP8
You came across FP8 in this newsletter already, so I thought of explaining the term.
FP8 is an 8-bit floating point number format. Most models store numbers in 16 bits (FP16 or BF16), so FP8 uses half the memory for the same data.

Of course, there is a trade-off for this and that trade-off is precision, since fewer bits means rougher numbers. For things like the KV cache, the "short-term memory" of a chat, the quality loss is usually small and the memory savings are big. That's why llama.cpp 1.0 adding FP8 KV caches matters on consumer GPUs.
⚡ Quick Tip
Not sure which model to pull next? If you have uv installed, you can run whichllm without installing anything:
uvx whichllm@latest
It checks your hardware and gives you a ranked list of models that will actually fit. If your integrated GPU or unified memory gets detected wrong, use --vram to set the limits yourself.

items.title: Pop!_OS 26.04 LTS Is Out: Here's What a Year of COSMIC Work Gets You
items.summary: Pop!_OS 26.04 LTS is based on Ubuntu 26.04 with Linux 7.2 and COSMIC 1.11. You get a redesigned store, automatic updates and a frosted glass look.
items.body:
System76's COSMIC desktop environment took more than three years to build before it became the default desktop of Pop!_OS 24.04 LTS last year. Since then, they have regularly put out point releases that have added new improvements.

All that is thanks to a sustained development effort and constant user feedback integration.

As for Pop!_OS, it builds its LTS releases on top of Ubuntu's, following a hybrid release path where users upgrade key system components when a new version arrives.

And, if that got you thinking, "I gotta try their latest release," well, then you are in luck as they have just announced the Pop!_OS 26.04 LTS release. It is based on Ubuntu 26.04 LTS and is available in multiple flavors, covering both x86_64 and ARM systems.

Pop!_OS 26.04 LTS

📋

Upgrades from 24.04 LTS to 26.04 LTS will be made available in December.

Before you decide on it, here are some changes in this release that are worth knowing about. Several of them already reached Pop!_OS 24.04 LTS through regular COSMIC updates, and the new release brings them together with a newer base.

1. Linux 7.2

The Pop!_OS 26.04 LTS release is powered by this kernel, more specifically, Linux 7.2.15, which is a point release.

It brings niceties like a scheduler feature that groups related tasks onto cores sharing the same last-level cache that can help latency-sensitive work and games on processors with more than one cache domain.

Laptop owners get support for more ASUS ROG and TUF Gaming models, battery charge limiting on Lenovo machines, and webcams on some Ryzen laptops.

AMDGPU gains early HDMI 2.1 support, and Realtek USB Ethernet adapters now handle 10 Gbit speeds and energy-efficient Ethernet.

2. COSMIC upgrades

For the desktop, COSMIC 1.11 is included that tweaks how windows behave. A fullscreen window now stays fullscreen when you move it to another workspace, and sticky windows stay on top of fullscreen ones.

Finding apps is quicker too, since you can start typing in the workspace overview, and it brings up the launcher or the app library, depending on what you pick in COSMIC Settings.

You can even neatly stack windows to get quick access to a group of apps from the same tiled layout. Just ensure that you drag and drop the windows only when the "Stack Windows" dialogue comes up.

Then there is Frosted Glass, a visual addition that arrived with COSMIC 1.3 and applies across the desktop. You can tweak it to be a nearly opaque look, a see-through one, or a subtle and balanced one.

3. Better store app

The COSMIC Store has been fully redesigned, and pages now open right away because it no longer refreshes updates each time you switch pages, reusing what it already loaded.

Startup is also quicker because it keeps its Explore results saved on disk, and it now pulls from all the added software sources at the same time. A new rpm-ostree backend is also available.

4. Monitoring made easy

Included as part of a fresh installation is the new COSMIC System Monitor app that puts CPU, memory, GPU, disk, and network usage on a single page along with applications and processes.

Each resource lists the process using the most of it, and opening one brings up charts next to the processes behind it. The app is built with COSMIC's own toolkit and blends in well with the rest of the desktop.

When I tried using it on a virtual machine, it bugged out badly, showing me artifacts when I launched or moved the app; this shouldn't be an issue on bare metal.

5. File manager tweaks

The file manager, COSMIC Files, has received a number of changes since the 24.04 launch, starting with the ability to open several folders in separate tabs and drag and drop those tabs around.

Right-clicking now gives you "Move to" and "Copy to" options, and holding Shift there copies an item's path. You can also paste images, videos, and text straight from the clipboard.

Network locations can be typed into the path bar and completed with Tab, and the Recents page can be switched off or cleared. Text files get previews as well, and deleting from the Trash folder now calls for a confirmation first.

6. Automatic system updates

Running automatic system updates is possible now; you can either switch it on during the initial setup on a fresh installation or later under the "System & accounts" page in Settings.

Inside the "System & application updates" entry, update notifications can be set to Disabled, Daily, Weekly, or Monthly, with granular controls for fine-tuning when the updates themselves run.

7. Constellations theming

Finally, if you go into the "Desktop" page in Settings or right-click on the desktop and select "Desktop appearance..." then click on "Appearance," you get access to the Constellations.

These are the set of bundled looks that cover the fonts, icons, accent colors, and wallpaper in one pick. You could say these are similar to Global Themes on KDE Plasma if you want to draw a parallel.

Dark and Light each have a set of their own to pick from, and clicking one swaps the wallpaper and accent color on the spot, with the window borders following along.

If you go for the plain ones with the COSMIC branding, even the dock icons turn single color. You can also have it switch between the two automatically, and each pick keeps whatever you set for it.

And if none of them suit you, there's an "Import theme" button for bringing in your own.

items.title: After 29 Years of Konsole, There's a New KDE Terminal and I Took It for a Spin
items.summary: KDE has a new modern terminal in works. It has a Ghostty connection, and it offers GPU acceleration. Take a look at it in this hands-on review.
items.body:
KDE has a new terminal, and no, it's not a Konsole update. It's called Kwi (pronounced "kwee"). It's built on Ghostty's terminal library, renders on your GPU and is made for KDE Plasma from scratch.

Version 0.1.0 is out so I took it for a test ride. I ran it in a CachyOS virtual machine with KDE Plasma (of course), so treat this as a feature tour and not a performance review.

If videos are your thing, I've covered the same features here on our YouTube channel:

Subscribe to It's FOSS YouTube Channel

Why another terminal when KDE has Konsole?

Kwi has tabs and a single menu button

Konsole has been around for 29 years. It's also one of the most customizable terminals you can use on Linux. So, why build a new one?

I would say that speed is a big part of the answer. Konsole is built on Qt Widgets and draws on the CPU. Kwi uses Qt Quick, which lets it render on the GPU through Vulkan or OpenGL.

Its developer, Eike Hein, claims that Kwi is 3 to 35 times faster than Konsole, depending on the benchmark. I haven't verified those numbers, and frankly, the numbers don't tell you everything about everyday use, but they do hint at what the project is aiming for.

The other part is Ghostty. Now, Kwi doesn't use the Ghostty app itself. It uses libghostty-vt, the library that handles terminal parsing behind the scenes.

The interface on top is pure KDE. It's built with the Kirigami framework and follows KDE's latest design guidelines. It also picks up your Plasma color scheme automatically, so it blends well with the rest of your KDE Plasma desktop.

💡

Fun fact: The name comes from 귀신 (gwisin or kwisin), the Korean word for ghost. Look at the little terminal ghost in Kwi logo and its connection with Ghost and Ghostty will start making sense.

Exploring Kwi and its features

Click the menu button and you will see the Configure Kwi option. This is where you can tweak the looks of the terminal.

Menu -> Configure Kwi

Change the font

By default, Kwi uses your system's fixed-width font. If you want something else, uncheck Use system fixed-width font. Then choose your font and its size.

The terminal behind the settings window updates live. That makes it easy to find something comfortable.

Uncheck the system font option to pick your own font

Change the colors

In the Colors section, the Window option controls the appearance of the app itself. You can switch between Breeze Light, Breeze Dark and the other available schemes.

The Terminal dropdown below it changes the colors inside the terminal.

Window and terminal colors are set separately

Your Konsole color schemes work here

Here's good news for longtime KDE users. Kwi works with Konsole color schemes, so your favorite theme doesn't have to stay behind.

Download a Konsole color scheme from the KDE Store. In Kwi's settings, click the three-dot button next to the Terminal dropdown, choose Import and select the downloaded file.

Use the three-dot menu to import a color scheme

The imported scheme now appears in the Terminal dropdown. I imported Gruvbox in the test here.

The imported Gruvbox scheme in the list

Make it transparent, with blur

If you like a see-through terminal, use the background opacity slider on the Appearance page. There's a Blur checkbox next to it.

Background opacity and blur options

However, the checkbox won't give you the frosted glass look if Plasma's own blur effect is disabled. To enable it, open System Settings -> Animations and click the Desktop Effects button.

Open Desktop Effects from the Animations page

Enable Blur here and hit Apply.

Enable Plasma's blur effect

Now go back to Kwi's Appearance settings and enable Blur there too. You get the frosted look everyone is going gaga over these days.

Transparent Kwi without blur (left) and with blur (right)

Move the tab bar

You can move the tab bar to the top or bottom of the window. Konsole lets you do this too, so nothing extraordinary here. There's also an option to hide the tab bar when only one tab is open.

Tab bar can be at the top or the bottom

Control the behavior

The Behavior page controls what happens when another application opens Kwi. You can choose between a new window and a new tab.

You can also copy mouse-selected text to the clipboard automatically, and choose whether opening a link requires Ctrl+click. There's an even nicer way to open links, which I'll show you in a minute.

Window, clipboard and link behavior

Limit the scrollback and change the cursor

In the Terminal section, you can set the scrollback history. On my installation, it was set to unlimited. I prefer limiting it to something like 10,000 lines, which should usually be enough.

You can also change the cursor shape to a block, beam or underline and decide whether it blinks.

Scrollback history and cursor settings

Create presets

A preset is basically a saved terminal profile. The easiest way to create one is to duplicate an existing preset from the three-dot menu.

Duplicate an existing preset to create a new one

Give it a name, a command to run and a starting folder. You can set environment variables for it too.

In my case, I made one called Bash Shell. It runs /bin/bash and starts in my home directory. You can open a new tab with a preset from Menu -> New Tab with Preset, or make it the default for new sessions.

Bash Shell is now the default preset

Customize keyboard shortcuts

Keyboard shortcuts get their own page in the settings. You can filter the list and change the shortcuts to suit your workflow.

Keyboard shortcuts have their own page

A few handy features

The settings are mostly what you'd expect from a KDE application. Some of the features outside them are rather more interesting.

Make the terminal read-only

Go to Menu -> Edit -> Read-Only Terminal. This blocks keyboard input, so you won't accidentally type into a terminal that's running something important.

Okay, it's not unique to Kwi. Other terminals offer this feature too, but it's good to have.

Menu -> Edit -> Read-Only Terminal

Find and open links

This is my favorite little feature. If your terminal output has lots of links, go to Menu -> Output -> Open Link.

Menu -> Output -> Open Link

You get a small dialog that lists the links on your screen. Type to search, select the one you want and press Enter to open it in your default browser. No need to hunt through the output with your mouse.

Search the links on your screen

Select text with the keyboard

Press Ctrl+Shift+D or go to Menu -> Edit -> Keyboard Selection Mode. Now you can move around the terminal output with your keyboard.

Menu -> Edit -> Keyboard Selection Mode

Use Ctrl+Shift and the arrow keys to select text, then press Enter to copy it. Paste it in the terminal with Ctrl+Shift+V, or use the usual paste shortcut in another application.

Text selected without touching the mouse

View images in the terminal

Kwi supports the Kitty image protocol. I used the Yazi file manager to browse a folder of wallpapers, and the previews appeared right inside the terminal.

Image previews with Yazi in Kwi

Kwi's announcement also lists support for font ligatures, Nerd Font icon scaling, the Kitty keyboard protocol and progress indicators, along with accessibility improvements for screen readers. I didn't test these individually.

Getting Kwi on your Linux

Kwi is still very, very new. Keep your expectations low and expect bugs. Explore it as an experimentation for now.

The easiest option is Kwi's Flatpak package from Flathub. If you have Flatpak set up with the Flathub repository, use this command to install Kwi:

flatpak install flathub org.kde.kwi

Kwi is available on Flathub

If you run into bugs, report them on KDE Bugzilla under kwi. That's one way to help the Linux ecosystem.

Wrapping up

Kwi was introduced as an experiment. It has since passed the KDE Review process and is now an official KDE project. That doesn't mean it's replacing Konsole, though. No such decision has been announced.

It also has fewer features than Konsole. Split panes are the obvious gap if you use them. They are planned, but not here yet.

blocks.text: KDE has a new terminal, and no, it's not a Konsole update. It's called Kwi (pronounced "kwee"). It's built on Ghostty's terminal library, renders on your GPU and is made for KDE Plasma from scratch.
Version 0.1.0 is out so I took it for a test ride. I ran it in a CachyOS virtual machine with KDE Plasma (of course), so treat this as a feature tour and not a performance review.
If videos are your thing, I've covered the same features here on our YouTube channel:
Subscribe to It's FOSS YouTube Channel
Why another terminal when KDE has Konsole?

blocks.alt: Kwi terminal on KDE Plasma with arrows pointing to its tab bar and menu button

blocks.text: Kwi has tabs and a single menu button
Konsole has been around for 29 years. It's also one of the most customizable terminals you can use on Linux. So, why build a new one?
I would say that speed is a big part of the answer. Konsole is built on Qt Widgets and draws on the CPU. Kwi uses Qt Quick, which lets it render on the GPU through Vulkan or OpenGL.

Its developer, Eike Hein, claims that Kwi is 3 to 35 times faster than Konsole, depending on the benchmark. I haven't verified those numbers, and frankly, the numbers don't tell you everything about everyday use, but they do hint at what the project is aiming for.
The other part is Ghostty. Now, Kwi doesn't use the Ghostty app itself. It uses libghostty-vt, the library that handles terminal parsing behind the scenes.

The interface on top is pure KDE. It's built with the Kirigami framework and follows KDE's latest design guidelines. It also picks up your Plasma color scheme automatically, so it blends well with the rest of your KDE Plasma desktop.
Fun fact: The name comes from 귀신 (gwisin or kwisin), the Korean word for ghost. Look at the little terminal ghost in Kwi logo and its connection with Ghost and Ghostty will start making sense.
Exploring Kwi and its features
Click the menu button and you will see the Configure Kwi option. This is where you can tweak the looks of the terminal.

blocks.alt: Kwi menu with arrows pointing to the menu button and the Configure Kwi option

blocks.text: Menu -> Configure Kwi
Change the font
By default, Kwi uses your system's fixed-width font. If you want something else, uncheck Use system fixed-width font. Then choose your font and its size.
The terminal behind the settings window updates live. That makes it easy to find something comfortable.

blocks.alt: Kwi Appearance settings with arrows pointing to the system font checkbox and the font selector

blocks.text: Uncheck the system font option to pick your own font
Change the colors
In the Colors section, the Window option controls the appearance of the app itself. You can switch between Breeze Light, Breeze Dark and the other available schemes.
The Terminal dropdown below it changes the colors inside the terminal.

blocks.alt: Kwi color settings with an arrow pointing to the Window color scheme selector

blocks.text: Window and terminal colors are set separately
Your Konsole color schemes work here
Here's good news for longtime KDE users. Kwi works with Konsole color schemes, so your favorite theme doesn't have to stay behind.
Download a Konsole color scheme from the KDE Store. In Kwi's settings, click the three-dot button next to the Terminal dropdown, choose Import and select the downloaded file.

blocks.alt: Three-dot menu next to the Terminal color scheme selector with arrows pointing to the button and the Import option

blocks.text: Use the three-dot menu to import a color scheme
The imported scheme now appears in the Terminal dropdown. I imported Gruvbox in the test here.

blocks.alt: List of terminal color schemes in Kwi with an arrow pointing to Gruvbox

blocks.text: The imported Gruvbox scheme in the list
Make it transparent, with blur
If you like a see-through terminal, use the background opacity slider on the Appearance page. There's a Blur checkbox next to it.

blocks.alt: Kwi Appearance settings with arrows pointing to the opacity slider and the Blur checkbox

blocks.text: Background opacity and blur options
However, the checkbox won't give you the frosted glass look if Plasma's own blur effect is disabled. To enable it, open System Settings -> Animations and click the Desktop Effects button.

blocks.alt: Animations page in Plasma System Settings with an arrow pointing to the Desktop Effects button

blocks.text: Open Desktop Effects from the Animations page
Enable Blur here and hit Apply.

blocks.alt: Desktop Effects settings with arrows pointing to the Blur effect and the Apply button

blocks.text: Enable Plasma's blur effect
Now go back to Kwi's Appearance settings and enable Blur there too. You get the frosted look everyone is going gaga over these days.

blocks.alt: A transparent Kwi window without blur on the left and with blur on the right

blocks.text: Transparent Kwi without blur (left) and with blur (right)
Move the tab bar
You can move the tab bar to the top or bottom of the window. Konsole lets you do this too, so nothing extraordinary here. There's also an option to hide the tab bar when only one tab is open.

blocks.alt: Kwi tab bar settings with an arrow pointing to the Position selector

blocks.text: Tab bar can be at the top or the bottom
Control the behavior
The Behavior page controls what happens when another application opens Kwi. You can choose between a new window and a new tab.
You can also copy mouse-selected text to the clipboard automatically, and choose whether opening a link requires Ctrl+click. There's an even nicer way to open links, which I'll show you in a minute.

blocks.alt: Kwi Behavior settings with arrows pointing to the window, clipboard and link options

blocks.text: Window, clipboard and link behavior
Limit the scrollback and change the cursor
In the Terminal section, you can set the scrollback history. On my installation, it was set to unlimited. I prefer limiting it to something like 10,000 lines, which should usually be enough.
You can also change the cursor shape to a block, beam or underline and decide whether it blinks.

blocks.alt: Kwi Terminal settings with arrows pointing to the scrollback limit and the cursor shape

blocks.text: Scrollback history and cursor settings
Create presets
A preset is basically a saved terminal profile. The easiest way to create one is to duplicate an existing preset from the three-dot menu.

blocks.alt: Three-dot menu in the Presets settings with an arrow pointing to Duplicate

blocks.text: Duplicate an existing preset to create a new one
Give it a name, a command to run and a starting folder. You can set environment variables for it too.

In my case, I made one called Bash Shell. It runs /bin/bash and starts in my home directory. You can open a new tab with a preset from Menu -> New Tab with Preset, or make it the default for new sessions.

blocks.alt: Presets settings with arrows pointing to the default preset and the preset being edited

blocks.text: Bash Shell is now the default preset
Customize keyboard shortcuts
Keyboard shortcuts get their own page in the settings. You can filter the list and change the shortcuts to suit your workflow.

blocks.alt: Keyboard shortcuts page in Kwi settings

blocks.text: Keyboard shortcuts have their own page
A few handy features
The settings are mostly what you'd expect from a KDE application. Some of the features outside them are rather more interesting.
Make the terminal read-only
Go to Menu -> Edit -> Read-Only Terminal. This blocks keyboard input, so you won't accidentally type into a terminal that's running something important.
Okay, it's not unique to Kwi. Other terminals offer this feature too, but it's good to have.

blocks.alt: Kwi Edit menu with an arrow pointing to Read-Only Terminal

blocks.text: Menu -> Edit -> Read-Only Terminal
Find and open links
This is my favorite little feature. If your terminal output has lots of links, go to Menu -> Output -> Open Link.

blocks.alt: Kwi Output menu with an arrow pointing to Open Link

blocks.text: Menu -> Output -> Open Link

You get a small dialog that lists the links on your screen. Type to search, select the one you want and press Enter to open it in your default browser. No need to hunt through the output with your mouse.

blocks.alt: Link picker dialog in Kwi with an arrow pointing to the search field

blocks.text: Search the links on your screen
Select text with the keyboard
Press Ctrl+Shift+D or go to Menu -> Edit -> Keyboard Selection Mode. Now you can move around the terminal output with your keyboard.

blocks.alt: Kwi Edit menu with an arrow pointing to Keyboard Selection Mode

blocks.text: Menu -> Edit -> Keyboard Selection Mode
Use Ctrl+Shift and the arrow keys to select text, then press Enter to copy it. Paste it in the terminal with Ctrl+Shift+V, or use the usual paste shortcut in another application.

blocks.alt: A line of text selected in Kwi with an arrow pointing to the selection

blocks.text: Text selected without touching the mouse
View images in the terminal
Kwi supports the Kitty image protocol. I used the Yazi file manager to browse a folder of wallpapers, and the previews appeared right inside the terminal.

blocks.alt: Yazi file manager showing an image preview inside Kwi

blocks.text: Image previews with Yazi in Kwi

Kwi's announcement also lists support for font ligatures, Nerd Font icon scaling, the Kitty keyboard protocol and progress indicators, along with accessibility improvements for screen readers. I didn't test these individually.
Getting Kwi on your Linux
Kwi is still very, very new. Keep your expectations low and expect bugs. Explore it as an experimentation for now.
The easiest option is Kwi's Flatpak package from Flathub. If you have Flatpak set up with the Flathub repository, use this command to install Kwi:
flatpak install flathub org.kde.kwi

blocks.alt: Kwi page on Flathub with an arrow pointing to the Install button

blocks.text: Kwi is available on Flathub
If you run into bugs, report them on KDE Bugzilla under kwi. That's one way to help the Linux ecosystem.
Wrapping up

Kwi was introduced as an experiment. It has since passed the KDE Review process and is now an official KDE project. That doesn't mean it's replacing Konsole, though. No such decision has been announced.
It also has fewer features than Konsole. Split panes are the obvious gap if you use them. They are planned, but not here yet.

Personally, I like where this is going. Kwi felt fast even in my virtual machine. It blends well with KDE Plasma and already has some useful features, especially the link picker and the keyboard selection mode.
I wouldn't ask you to drop Konsole for it today. While Kwi develops further, you can explore a few Konsole tweaks or look at other terminal emulators for Linux.
💬 Now, it's up to you. Would you switch from Konsole to Kwi once it matures? Let me know in the comments.

items.title: No One is Using Real Firefox Browser on iPhones (Blame it on Apple)
items.summary: The EU told Apple to open up. Apple said "fine." Then it published its own set of conditions so that complying in practice is nearly impossible for Mozilla Firefox.
items.body:
If you use Firefox on an iPhone, you have never used the "real Firefox".

I know that sounds overly dramatic, but it's technically true. The Firefox you get on iPhone or iPad, doesn't use the Gecko engine that is the core of the Firefox browser.

Here's why that happens.

Mozilla accuses Apple of playing dirty

The EU Digital Markets Act (DMA), the law that forces big platforms to open up, started requiring Apple to let people choose their default browser in 2024. It also required Apple to allow alternative browser engines on iOS.

Apple published its own set of conditions for anyone wanting to bring a different engine, and at the time Mozilla warned those rules made it "as painful as possible" for Gecko.

Basically, Apple complied with the rules on paper, then wrote its own set of fine print so that complying in practice is nearly impossible.

Mozilla says that to bring its own engine, Gecko (the engine that powers real Firefox on every other platform), it cannot simply update the Firefox app people already use.

Apple's conditions would force Mozilla to build a second, completely separate Firefox app. Then every existing user would have to download that new app, move their bookmarks, passwords and history across, and manually switch over. No user is going to take that much trouble just for updating a browser.

So Firefox cannot use its own Gecko browser engine, the core software that actually renders web pages. And it's not just Firefox. Nearly three years since Apple introduced these conditions in the EU, not one developer has been able to launch a non-WebKit browser on iOS.

the open door feels more like a "trap door."

Apple's mischief is not a surprise. This is the same company that rejected the Epic Games Store app twice in Europe before approving it, and that only happens when regulators are watching.

It matters more than you think

When you install Firefox, Brave or even Chrome on an iPhone, you're getting the same WebKit engine Safari uses at its core. iPhones and iPads are the only major platforms where this happens. Even Apple's own macOS lets you run real, Gecko-powered Firefox.

Mozilla says it has been working behind the scenes since the DMA took effect to test and improve Apple's conditions so it can bring the Gecko browser engine and thus the real Firefix to iOS users. Those efforts have, in Mozilla's words, so far largely failed.

Meanwhile, Firefox on iPhone keeps growing. Mozilla says millions of people have picked Firefox from the EU's choice screen since 2024, and daily use on iOS has doubled.

It is an indication that people want to choose their browser and not rely on Apple's Safari.

What happens next?

Mozilla says it will keep pushing for the real change because Apple's conditions remain unworkable and that compliance on paper is just a way to circumvent the regulations.

The next move likely belongs to EU regulators, who have already investigated Apple's browser choice screen design and taken preliminary issue with the conditions Apple attaches to its EU concessions.

Until then, the "real Firefox" stays off the iOS devices.

items.title: CachyOS Just Made One of Linux’s Biggest Gaming Problems Way Easier
items.summary: CachyOS Now Has a Separate Kernel Just for Easy Anti-Cheat Games. This EAC kernel gets its own boot entry, while a recovery environment for Btrfs snapshots is also provided.
items.body:
CachyOS is a distro pick that suits both power users and gamers alike. The installer offers 17+ desktop environments to pick from, and gamers get a Handheld Edition for devices like the Steam Deck and ROG Ally.

Based on Arch Linux, it ships its own kernel and package builds for specific CPUs, while the installer comes as a GUI or a command-line version.

CachyOS has now put out its sixth release of the year, and this one changes how the system boots, recovers, and installs software.

The November Release

CachyOS now has a dedicated kernel for games that use Epic's Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC) Linux v2. EAC checks the boot chain before it lets a game run, and the new linux-cachyos-eac kernel is signed with the CachyOS key.

Don't worry, it gets a dedicated boot entry, while your regular ones stay untouched, with the eac-setup script handling the bootloader configuration. Because DKMS modules don't load on this kernel, NVIDIA, ZFS and r8125 come as prebuilt packages for it.

Then there's cachyos-recovery, a rescue image that lives on the EFI partition and can be launched from the bootloader menu or directly from UEFI without a live USB.

From its menu, you can boot any Btrfs snapshot with a writable root to check it first and roll back once you're happy with it. The rollback also runs from a desktop notification.

It works without Snapper and supports LUKS-encrypted disks. The package is cachyos-recovery, with a cachyos-recovery-legacy variant specifically for BIOS machines.

Similarly, Package Installer, the software manager, reaches v2.0 with a new UI. It can now handle AUR, Flatpak and AppImage packages, and each one is opt-in.

Before an AUR build runs, you can read the PKGBUILD and install scripts, and a static analysis step highlights what deserves a closer look. Updates come with a diff against the installed version.

CachyOS Settings, the package holding CachyOS's tuning configs, brings backsystemd-oomd, the out-of-memory killer, and enables it by default. It steps in based on swap usage and skips the user session.

The new cachyos-drm-awaiter helper replaces early KMS and the nvidia-module-loader. Early KMS used to initialize the graphics driver during the boot process, allowing CachyOS to switch to the display's native resolution much earlier.

Now, the helper holds the login screen back until the graphics driver has loaded, and that applies to any driver rather than only NVIDIA's. If loading fails, a QR code shows up on screen.

chwd, the hardware detection tool, drops early KMS to match, and existing users need to run sudo sudo chwd -a -f after updating to apply the change.

Calamares (the GUI installer) uses the CLI installer's gucc library for the initramfs, machine-id, and post-install steps, and the rest is being moved over step by step. The CLI installer itself was refactored onto the same library.

Plymouth, the boot splash, is now optional, and the rEFInd + AI SDK bootloader option is gone. CachyOS can also run on the Windows Subsystem for Linux now through a new image.

And finally, the kernel moves to Linux 7.3.5, with NVIDIA 620.73.04 and Mesa 26.3.1 also being included. The full changelog is available in the release blog post.

Download CachyOS

The Desktop Edition ISOs have been updated to reflect the changes in this new release. If you are looking to try it for the first time, then this is the pick for you.

cachyOS

Existing users can upgrade to this release by running the following command:

sudo pacman -Syu

items.title: Your Linux Laptop Won't Suspend? Here's What You Can Do
items.summary: When a Linux laptop refuses to sleep, the first instinct should be to check what's stopping it. Here's a troubleshoot guide for your reference.
items.body:
You close the lid and the laptop keeps running. Or you leave it alone for an hour and it never goes to sleep. Often nothing is broken. The cause is a program that asked systemd to hold off sleep.

That request is called an inhibitor lock. In this article, you'll list the locks on your system, read what each one blocks, tell a lock that stops a suspend from one that only delays it, and close the program that holds it.

Every command here works on any distribution that uses systemd. I ran them on an Ubuntu 26.04 desktop virtual machine with GNOME, which ships systemd 259.

What an inhibitor lock is

A program takes an inhibitor lock from systemd-logind, the systemd service that handles sleep, shutdown and the power keys. The lock says what the program wants to hold back, why, and for how long.

A backup tool might hold a lock while it copies files, so the laptop doesn't suspend halfway through. A video player might hold one so the screen doesn't go idle during a movie. When the program exits, its lock goes away with it.

The problem starts when a program holds a lock it no longer needs, or holds a stronger lock than it should.

List every inhibitor lock

The systemd-inhibit command lists the active locks. It needs no root.

systemd-inhibit --list

To have a lock to clear later in this article, I first started a stand-in backup job wrapped in systemd-inhibit. It holds a block lock on sleep and shows up as "Backup script". Everything else in the list below came from the system itself.

WHO                          UID  USER     PID  COMM            WHAT                                                     WHY                                                         MODE
Backup script                0    root     4952 systemd-inhibit sleep                                                    Copying files to the NAS                                    block
ModemManager                 0    root     1322 ModemManager    sleep                                                    ModemManager needs to reset devices                         delay
NetworkManager               0    root     1196 NetworkManager  sleep                                                    NetworkManager needs to turn off networks                   delay
Realtime Kit                 0    root     1497 rtkit-daemon    sleep                                                    Demote realtime scheduling and stop canary.                 delay
UPower                       0    root     2006 upowerd         sleep                                                    Pause device polling                                        delay
Unattended Upgrades Shutdown 0    root     1365 unattended-upgr shutdown                                                 Stop ongoing upgrades or perform upgrades before shutdown   delay
GNOME Shell                  1000 demouser 3538 gnome-shell     sleep                                                    GNOME needs to lock the screen                              delay
GNOME Shell                  1000 demouser 3538 gnome-shell     sleep                                                    GNOME needs to save screen time data                        delay
demouser                     1000 demouser 3683 gsd-power       handle-lid-switch                                        External monitor attached or configuration changed recently block
demouser                     1000 demouser 3682 gsd-media-keys  handle-power-key:handle-suspend-key:handle-hibernate-key GNOME handling keypresses                                   block
demouser                     1000 demouser 3682 gsd-media-keys  sleep                                                    GNOME handling keypresses                                   delay
demouser                     1000 demouser 3683 gsd-power       sleep                                                    GNOME needs to lock the screen                              delay

12 inhibitors listed.

Here is what each column tells you.

• WHO is the name the program gave itself.

• PID and COMM are the process that holds the lock. You'll use the PID later to find and close it.

• WHAT is what the lock holds back.

• WHY is the reason the program gave.

• MODE says whether the lock blocks the action or only delays it.

Read the WHAT column

The WHAT column tells you which problem a lock can cause. These are the values that matter for suspend and idle.

• sleep covers suspend and hibernate. A block lock here stops the laptop from suspending at all.

• idle stops the system from treating your session as idle. That blocks anything that waits for idle, such as automatic suspend after a timeout. This is the usual reason a laptop ignores its idle timer.

• handle-lid-switch takes over the lid. While a program holds it, systemd doesn't act when you close the lid.

• handle-power-key, handle-suspend-key and handle-hibernate-key do the same for those keys. Desktops often hold them because they handle the keys themselves, so these locks are normal.

• shutdown covers power off and reboot.

A lock can list more than one value, separated by colons, such as sleep:shutdown.

Tell a block lock from a delay lock

The MODE column has two values.

A block lock stops the action for as long as the program holds it. Only a privileged user can override it. This is the kind that leaves a laptop awake.

A delay lock only holds the action back for a short time, so the program can finish something first. A chat app might save its state before the laptop sleeps. When the time runs out, systemd suspends anyway. The limit is InhibitDelayMaxSec= in /etc/systemd/logind.conf. The commented default in that file is 5 seconds.

Delay locks exist only for sleep and shutdown. When I tried to take one for idle, systemd refused it.

systemd-inhibit --what=idle --mode=delay --who=test --why=test true

Failed to inhibit: Delay inhibitors only supported for shutdown and sleep

Most of the list above is delay locks from GNOME, NetworkManager, ModemManager, Realtime Kit and UPower. They rarely cause trouble. When your laptop won't sleep, look for a block lock on sleep, idle or handle-lid-switch.

Show only the block locks

On a desktop, the list can run to a dozen lines. Add --mode=block to see only the locks that can stop an action.

systemd-inhibit --list --mode=block

WHO           UID  USER     PID  COMM            WHAT                                                     WHY                                                         MODE
Backup script 0    root     4952 systemd-inhibit sleep                                                    Copying files to the NAS                                    block
demouser      1000 demouser 3683 gsd-power       handle-lid-switch                                        External monitor attached or configuration changed recently block
demouser      1000 demouser 3682 gsd-media-keys  handle-power-key:handle-suspend-key:handle-hibernate-key GNOME handling keypresses                                   block

3 inhibitors listed.

Here is what each of the three does.

Backup script is the stand-in job. It holds a block lock on sleep, so the laptop can't suspend while it runs.

gsd-power is GNOME's power manager. It holds a block lock on handle-lid-switch. Its reason reads "External monitor attached or configuration changed recently". GNOME takes this lock while an external monitor is attached and for a short time after the display setup changes, so the laptop keeps running when you close the lid. If your laptop stays on when you close the lid, check for this lock first.

gsd-media-keys is GNOME's key handler. It blocks systemd from acting on the power, suspend and hibernate keys because GNOME handles those keys itself. This lock is normal on a GNOME desktop.

You might expect --what=sleep to narrow the list the same way. On systemd 259 it doesn't. systemd-inhibit --list --what=idle printed every lock on my test machine, including the ones on sleep and shutdown. The man page doesn't say that --list filters by WHAT, so read the WHAT column yourself.

Find and close the program that holds a block lock

Take the PID from the lock you want to clear. Look at the full command line of that process.

ps -p 4952 -o pid,comm,args

    PID COMMAND         COMMAND
   4952 systemd-inhibit systemd-inhibit --what=sleep --who=Backup script --why=Copying files to the NAS --mode=block sleep 300

In this case the lock comes from a script that wraps a job in systemd-inhibit, so the command line shows the job it's running. When COMM shows a normal application, such as a browser or a media player, that application holds the lock itself.

The cleanest fix is to close the program the way you normally would, or to change its own power setting. Some programs have their own setting that keeps the system awake. If the program is stuck, end it with its PID.

sudo kill 4952

List the locks again to confirm the lock is gone.

systemd-inhibit --list --mode=block

WHO      UID  USER     PID  COMM           WHAT                                                     WHY                                                         MODE
demouser 1000 demouser 3683 gsd-power      handle-lid-switch                                        External monitor attached or configuration changed recently block
demouser 1000 demouser 3682 gsd-media-keys handle-power-key:handle-suspend-key:handle-hibernate-key GNOME handling keypresses                                   block

2 inhibitors listed.

If the lock belongs to a system service, stop that service with systemctl instead of killing the process, so it doesn't start again and take a new lock.

Check whether a lock is really the cause

Inhibitor locks only apply when a suspend goes through systemd. That covers systemctl suspend, the suspend option in your desktop's menu, the lid and the idle timer.

To find out whether a lock is what keeps your laptop awake, suspend once with the lock checks turned off.

sudo systemctl suspend --check-inhibitors=no

If the laptop suspends now, a lock was the cause, and the steps above will find it. If it still doesn't suspend, the cause is outside systemd's locks. The kernel log from the failed attempt is the next place to look.

Conclusion

When a Linux laptop refuses to sleep, start with systemd-inhibit --list. Look for a block lock on sleep, idle or handle-lid-switch, find its process from the PID, and close that program or change its power setting. A delay lock only holds the suspend for a few seconds and is rarely the problem.

This is just one of the many systemd tools you can use for troubleshooting your Linux system.

New to Linux? These 4 systemd Tools Help You Fix Common Issues

Stop guessing, start investigating. Here are 4 systemd tools that make Linux troubleshooting easy.

It's FOSSNeville Ondara

Next time your laptop stays awake with the lid closed, run the list before you start digging through power settings.

In this case the lock comes from a script that wraps a job in systemd-inhibit, so the command line shows the job it's running. When COMM shows a normal application, such as a browser or a media player, that application holds the lock itself.

The cleanest fix is to close the program the way you normally would, or to change its own power setting. Some programs have their own setting that keeps the system awake. If the program is stuck, end it with its PID.
sudo kill 4952

Check whether a lock is really the cause
Inhibitor locks only apply when a suspend goes through systemd. That covers systemctl suspend, the suspend option in your desktop's menu, the lid and the idle timer.
To find out whether a lock is what keeps your laptop awake, suspend once with the lock checks turned off.

If the laptop suspends now, a lock was the cause, and the steps above will find it. If it still doesn't suspend, the cause is outside systemd's locks. The kernel log from the failed attempt is the next place to look.

When a Linux laptop refuses to sleep, start with systemd-inhibit --list. Look for a block lock on sleep, idle or handle-lid-switch, find its process from the PID, and close that program or change its power setting. A delay lock only holds the suspend for a few seconds and is rarely the problem.

items.title: My Hybrid AI System in Obsidian: Local and Cloud AI Integration
items.summary: Using AI with notes gives superpower to your notes. But should you give AI access to your knowledge base?
items.body:
AI is rapidly gaining popularity across various fields, and I've found that integrating it into a personal knowledge management system like Obsidian offers far more benefits than one might initially expect.

In this article, I'll show you exactly how I've enabled both local AI and cloud AI within Obsidian, configuring them for different vaults to suit my specific needs.

How I Choose AI

AI technology, while powerful, often comes with inherent privacy concerns.

When you opt for a corporate AI solution, which typically offers faster queries and results, you're risking your privacy.

On the other hand, if you decide to use local AI, it can be quite taxing and slow, especially on moderate hardware.

Given this dilemma, I asked myself: why not use both? With Obsidian, setting up such a workflow is surprisingly easy.

I personally use a local AI for my most private notes and journals, ensuring my personal thoughts remain entirely on my machine.

For my work-related documents and learning journeys, where speed and broader knowledge access are key, I leverage Gemini chat (because it's free). This approach gives me the best of both worlds: privacy where it matters most, and powerful cloud capabilities for everything else.

If you want more segregation, have separate vaults for your work and personal notes.

📋

It's worth noting that for local AI to work seamlessly and efficiently, a decent GPU is a crucial component.

Use Copilot for Obsidian extension

Don't go by the name. It's not exclusive to Microsoft Copilot.

To integrate AI directly into Obsidian, I rely on Copilot for Obsidian, a fantastic community extension. This plugin supports both local and cloud AI, and it even offers its own Plus features for those who want to enhance their experience further.

Here's how to install this extension in Obsidian:

Go to the Obsidian settings by pressing CTRL+,. Inside the settings, go to Community Plugins -> Browse.

Click on Browse

Search for Copilot and install the extension.

Install Copilot

Enable it right away using the Enable button.

Setting Gemini AI in Obsidian

Now that Copilot for Obsidian is installed, let me show how I configure Gemini AI within Obsidian.

Create API Key

Go to the Google AI Studio website. Click on Create API key button.

Create API Key

Here, give the key a name and click on Create a New Project.

Create a New Project

Give the project a name and click on Create Project

Create Project with a name

Now, click on Create Key.

Click on Create Key

Use the Copy key button to copy the API key.

Copy the API Key

Configure Obsidian Copilot

To configure Copilot, open Obsidian and go to settings (CTRL+,). Here, in the sidebar, scroll down and select Copilot.

In the copilot settings, go to the Basic tab, click on Set Keys button.

Click on Set Keys

Here, paste the copied API key into the designated field and then select your preferred Gemini model from the dropdown. I have added the Gemini 2.5 Flash model in this particular setup.

Add key and model

Set the default chat model to the added one.

Set default chat model

By now, Copilot should be ready and available in the ribbon menu. Simply click on its icon there to open it in the right sidebar.

Copilot in Sidebar

Follow the same setup for other AI providers like Claude, GPT, etc.

Setting up Local AI

The Copilot plugin isn't just for cloud AI; it can also be used to set up local AI directly within Obsidian.

🚧

Again, Local AI is a resource-intensive process. It's recommended to use higher models only if you have a dedicated GPU and sufficient RAM available.

Here, I'll explain how to get local AI working using Ollama.

Install Ollama

Ollama is a command-line tool that allows us to download and run open-source Large Language Models (LLMs) like Llama3, Phi-3, Mistral, CodeGamma, and many others, right on my local machine.

To run AI locally on Linux with Ollama, you should have a GPU on your system. While it's possible to run AI on a CPU, the experience won't be ideal. A GPU is highly recommended for better performance. If you have a TPU/NPU, that would be even better but I am not sure if Ollama would support all TPU/NPU.

For this tutorial, I'll be using the Llama3.2 3B model. Even though it can be taxing on a CPU-only machine, it still offers noticeably faster performance compared to larger models without a dedicated GPU.

You can, of course, choose other, heavier models based on your system's specifications.

To install Ollama, use the command:

curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh

Once Ollama is installed, it's a good idea to check if it's running correctly. By default, it operates on a specific port number on localhost.

To verify its status, open a web browser and enter:

localhost:11434

It should show the message, "Ollama is running".

Install llama3.2 3b model

Now that you have Ollama up and running, install the llama3.2 3b model using the command:

ollama run llama3.2:3b

This will download almost 2GB+ data and enable the model. Once the command execution is completed, you will be automatically entered to a llama prompt, where you can chat with the model from terminal.

To exit the prompt, use the command:

/bye

To stop the model, use the command:

ollama stop llama3.2:3b

Note the name of the AI

In a terminal, run the ollama command:

ollama list

This will list the installed models in your system. Copy the name of the llama3.2 model exactly as shown in the output.

Ollama List Models

Configure Obsidian Copilot

Open Obsidian and go to the Copilot settings as done for the Gemini method.

Here, go to the Model tab and select Add Model button.

Click on Add Model

Fill the fields appropriately. The Model Name, marked with a red asterisk, should be exactly the name you copied in the last step.

The Display name can be any identifiable name you choose. Set the provider to Ollama, and you can leave the Base URL and API key fields as their default values; there's no need to add anything there.

Add Ollama Model

You can enable Vision in Model Capabilities if you want to allow image additions to the chat.

Once you've filled everything out, you can press the Test button to check for any configuration errors. If no errors are reported, use the Add Model button to add this model to your available list.

Now, go back to the Basic tab and set the default chat model to Llama.

That's it! From now on, you can use the local AI to chat with your notes.

Using the AI interface

Copilot for Obsidian comes packed with a lot of cool features. Let's take a look at some of the cooler ones that you may find yourself using frequently.

Context aware chat

As we've seen, Copilot features a neat chat interface that appears in the right sidebar when enabled. This sidebar offers several cool options that can significantly improve your notes.

For example, by default, the current note is automatically selected as the context for your chat. However, by pressing the @ symbol, I can easily select multiple notes to serve as context for my conversation, allowing for more comprehensive and interconnected AI interactions.

Chat with multiple notes

Send images in chat

At times, you may want to chat along with a screenshot. For example, when I am writing some configs, I can take a screenshot of an error and ask the LLM what the error is right then and there.

If the model supports processing images, you can do this directly via the sidebar interface. This is shown in the recording below.

Chat with Images

Add chat to note

What is the use of an AI assistant if it cannot add content directly to your notes? Copy and paste is not always a good solution.

To solve this, each result in the sidebar has an Insert/Replace at cursor button. Clicking on it immediately adds the chat result to the exact place where your cursor is currently located in your note or document, making the workflow incredibly seamless.

Adding Chat Content to Note

Chat backups

Copilot extension adds all chat sessions to a dedicated folder (copilot/copilot-conversations) in your vault as standard Markdown documents. The chat file is cleanly structured in a simple format:

user: user's prompt
ai: ai reply

The best thing about this setup is that it is properly backlinked. A backlink to the chat note is available right within your active note, which is incredibly good for getting a quick refresh on your thought process later on.

Wrapping Up

Using AI in a note-taking application could be a controversial choice, and it is completely a user's personal choice. While AI can hallucinate and add wrong data, I never suggest someone use it for research purposes.

The core learning and note-taking should always be done manually, but you can leverage the power of AI to add some helpful context to your note. Also, you can use it to format your note into a better Personal Knowledge Management (PKM) format, as doing that completely manually is often just an unwanted burden.

Do you prefer using AI in your Obsidian? Feel free to mention your thoughts in the comments section.

Infisical

Your AI agents need API keys, but they shouldn’t hold them. Agent Vault brokers credentials at request time, so secrets never land in prompts or logs. Give AI agents access, not your secrets.

Newsletter Update: Software Previews

A few weeks ago, I stopped tagging AI-assisted projects in the newsletter as most projects now use AI in some capacity – and I can't be the arbiter of what is and isn't vibe coded.

This week, I'm adding hover previews (screenshots) to new software tiles in the web version of the newsletter. While not all vibe coded projects are identifiable by their design, many are – and so this will hopefully be the first of several tools deployed in the coming months to help you quickly judge for yourself which projects you'd rather avoid.

I'm adding similar functionality to the directory (which is also live today), but it'll take a few weeks to backfill existing apps.

Weekly Highlights

AI is ruining the internet. I haven't been shy in the past about my disdain for how AI has re-shaped online interactions, whether it's the influx of bot accounts on social media or the dozens of emails I receive each week that are all some form of the following:

Hi. I'm a big fan of This Week in Self-Hosted [sic] and thought you might be interested in a new project...

If it's a fit for the newsletter, great. If not, say the word and you won't hear from me again.

More specifically this week, though, I'm perturbed by how AI is closing off the open web after Reddit officially discontinued RSS feeds (they've been talking about it for months, but feeds finally stopped working this past Monday) and Last.fm announced API access will require a paid account starting in December.

Both of these announcements hit close to 127.0.0.1 given the number of platforms that rely on Reddit's feeds (mostly because of its dogsh*t interface) or Last.fm for the ability to scrobble streams from self-hosted music sources.

But as frustrated as I am with the changes, I can't say I don't understand them. Services are realizing that if they don't charge for their content, AI companies will happily profit off it for free.

If our goal was ever to create an open internet, we're officially moving backwards.

In other news and activity:

• Codeberg experienced downtime this week as a result of domain troubles that are still being sorted out with their registrar

• Two popular self-hosted projects were renamed – Hister (search) is now Nogon, and Edit Mind (video knowledge base) is now Orcah Studio

• OpenCloud announced they're restricting production releases to enterprise customers and limiting community users to rolling releases (similar to what Proxmox and others do)

• Infisical (disclosure: this week's sponsor) took some heat for paywalling custom roles in a recent patch release. Their founder responded to the backlash and acknowledged the lack of communication, but the paywall seems to be staying put.

• BookOrbit is scaring off third-party developers with restricted API routes, which the maintainer claims is to thwart cracked versions of the official app (please stop using this platform)

• NordPass released their annual report of the most common passwords, and (unsurprisingly) 123456 leads the pack (and apparently has for seven of the last eight years)

• FoxxMD, the maintainer of Multi-Scrobbler, is already working to help users migrate from Last.fm and needs some testers

• Redict, a popular fork of Redis created over licensing concerns, is being deprecated (and its maintainers are encouraging users to switch to Valkey instead)

• Wiki.js v3.0, which had been in development for years until its recent release, is somehow already on v3.5.0

• Manjaro Linux, a semi-popular Linux distribution, officially registered as a recognized non-profit in Germany

• Novel project ideas I stumbled upon: Turn DNS queries from ad-blocking platforms into a Galaga-style browser game; convert a tablet into a wall-mounted grandfather clock with notifications

Happy selfh.st/ing!

Meet Tunarr, a self-hosted platform for emulating custom TV channels. With Tunarr, users can recreate the broadcast TV experience with custom-scheduled channels of their own media that can be browsed via a traditional guide-like interface. Features include support for various media sources (local files, Jellyfin, Plex, Emby), advanced search and filters, filler content (commercials, music videos, etc.), and per-channel subtitles.

Preface commands with nohup (no hang up) to continue running them after exiting a terminal session. Upon completion, nohup will create a file titled nohup.out with the output of the command for completion verification.

$ nohup apt update
  nohup: ignoring input and appending output to 'nohup.out'

$ cat nohup.out
  ...
  Reading package lists...
  Building dependency tree...
  Reading state information...
  6 packages can be upgraded.

Preface commands with nohup (no hang up) to continue running them after exiting a terminal session. Upon completion, nohup will create a file titled nohup.out with the output of the command for completion verification.

$ nohup apt update
  nohup: ignoring input and appending output to 'nohup.out'

$ cat nohup.out
  ...
  Reading package lists...
  Building dependency tree...
  Reading state information...
  6 packages can be upgraded.
